title: Blog 1
content:
Exploring Amazon S3 and Its Application in Storing Book Documents and Images in the Cloud Library Management System 1. Overview of Amazon S3 Amazon S3 (Amazon Simple Storage Service) is an object storage service provided by AWS. This service allows users to store and retrieve various types of data, such as images, PDF documents, videos, backup files, and other content.
Unlike databases designed to manage structured information, Amazon S3 focuses on storing and managing data objects.
Basic Concepts of Amazon S3 Bucket: A container for storing objects. When using Amazon S3, we need to create a bucket before uploading files.
Object: Data stored in a bucket, such as a PDF file or a book cover image. Each object consists of data content and related information.
Object Key: The identifier of an object within a bucket.
For example, in a library system, files can be organized using Object Keys such as:
books/covers/book001.jpg books/pdfs/book001.pdf authors/submissions/book002.pdf This is an example of how data can be organized, not a confirmed storage structure in the project.
Storage Class: Amazon S3 provides various storage classes to meet different access requirements and optimize costs. The selection of a Storage Class should be based on usage frequency and data retrieval requirements. 2. File Storage Requirements in Cloud Library Cloud Library Management System is a group project designed to build a library management system and support users in reading books online.
In this system, data can be divided into two main categories.
Book Information Data Includes:
Book ID. Book title. Author. Category. Description. Other business-related information. This type of data can be managed using Amazon DynamoDB.
File-Based Data Includes:
Book cover images. PDF documents. Files uploaded during system usage. For the second category, Amazon S3 is a storage solution worth exploring because it is designed to manage objects rather than business data records.
Separating book information from file content also helps establish clearer responsibilities among different system components.
3. Combining Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB A suitable design approach for Cloud Library is to use Amazon DynamoDB to store business information and Amazon S3 to store book-related files.
For example, when a new book is added to the system:
The book cover image or PDF file is uploaded to an appropriate storage location. The system records the Object Key or reference information for the file. The book information is stored in DynamoDB. When users open the book details page, the application retrieves the book information and uses the file reference to display the appropriate content. With this approach, DynamoDB does not need to directly store the entire binary content of PDF files or book cover images.
During the development of Cloud Library, I had the opportunity to examine book data stored in DynamoDB tables and observe how the user interface displays the book catalog.
From this experience, I further explored the role of an object storage service such as Amazon S3 in managing file-based data components.
However, the actual file storage implementation still needs to be verified against the project’s configuration and source code.
4. Managing PDF Files and Book Cover Images For an online library application, book cover images and reading materials have different access requirements.
Book Cover Images Book cover images are commonly used when displaying the book catalog or book details pages.
If stored in Amazon S3, the application can reference the corresponding objects to retrieve and display images.
For content that is permitted to be publicly accessible, Amazon CloudFront can also be explored to distribute content efficiently while maintaining control over access to Amazon S3.
PDF Files Unlike book cover images, some PDF documents may require users to log in or meet specific access conditions before reading.
Therefore, when exploring document storage on Amazon S3, I need to pay attention to access permissions rather than allowing all users to download files directly by default.
Files Submitted by Authors Cloud Library provides a feature that allows authors to submit books for approval.
Files awaiting approval need to be managed separately to prevent documents from being publicly accessible before they are approved.
One possible design approach is to store these documents in a private storage area and grant access only to authorized components responsible for processing them.
5. Data Security on Amazon S3 While learning about Amazon S3, I realized that access management is a particularly important consideration.
Block Public Access Amazon S3 provides the Block Public Access mechanism to prevent unintended public access permissions.
For a library system, especially for documents that are not intended to be freely accessible, maintaining appropriate security configurations is essential.
IAM Policies and Bucket Policies These policies help control which identities or components are permitted to perform operations such as uploading, reading, or deleting objects.
Presigned URL A Presigned URL is a method of granting temporary access to a specific object without making the entire bucket publicly accessible.
For example, after the system verifies that a user has permission to read a document, the backend can generate a Presigned URL that allows the user to access the file for a specified period.
However, Presigned URLs must be protected because anyone who possesses a valid URL can use the access permissions granted by that URL.
Data Encryption Amazon S3 automatically encrypts new objects when they are stored. In addition to the default encryption mechanism, AWS also supports other encryption options to meet the security requirements of different systems.
Through these concepts, I realized that successfully uploading files is only the first step when using Amazon S3. Developers also need to consider how users access files and the scope of the permissions granted.
6. Cost and Data Organization Considerations In addition to security, cost is another factor that needs to be considered when using Amazon S3.
Costs may depend on storage capacity, the number of requests, storage classes, and data transfer activities.
For Cloud Library, the number of book cover images and PDF documents may increase as new books are added to the library. Therefore, proper data organization and management plans are necessary.
Some key points I learned while exploring Amazon S3 include:
Use clear naming conventions for Object Keys. Distinguish between publicly accessible files and files that require authentication. Validate file types and file sizes when users upload files. Do not grant public access to an entire bucket simply to display certain documents. Select appropriate Storage Classes based on access frequency. Monitor storage capacity and requests that generate costs. Consider data lifecycle policies when the system contains many files that are no longer in use. 7. Conclusion Amazon S3 is an object storage service that can meet various file management requirements in web applications, particularly for systems containing images and documents, such as Cloud Library Management System.
Through learning about Amazon S3, I gained a better understanding of the differences between storing business data in Amazon DynamoDB and storing files as objects.
In addition, I realized that storage design should be considered together with access permissions, data security, and usage costs.
In the future, I would like to continue exploring how to integrate Amazon S3 into the processes of uploading documents, displaying book cover images, and granting access permissions for reading PDF files in the library system.
I hope this article provides a useful perspective for those who are learning about Amazon S3 and how to combine object storage services with other components in real-world applications.

title: Blog 2
content:
Exploring Amazon Cognito and Its Application in User Authentication in the Cloud Library Management System Project 1. Overview of Amazon Cognito Amazon Cognito is an AWS service that supports identity management and user authentication for web and mobile applications.
Instead of building an entire authentication system from scratch, developers can use Amazon Cognito to implement features such as account registration, login, contact information verification, and password recovery.
Basic Components of Amazon Cognito User Pools: Manage user accounts and perform authentication.
Identity Pools: Provide temporary AWS credentials that allow applications to access AWS resources based on configured permissions.
Within the scope of the Cloud Library project, I focused on learning about and using Amazon Cognito User Pools.
2. User Pool and App Client When configuring Amazon Cognito, the first two components I needed to understand were User Pool and App Client.
User Pool A User Pool is a directory that manages the accounts of application users.
Depending on the configuration, users can register with their email addresses, verify their accounts, and log in using permitted authentication methods.
App Client An App Client is a configuration for an application that connects to a User Pool.
The App Client defines the authentication methods and related settings that the application can use.
In Cloud Library, I created a User Pool and an App Client in the AWS Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region, then used this configuration to test the system’s user account functionalities.
Through this step, I gained a better understanding of how applications connect to a managed authentication service on AWS.
3. Applying Amazon Cognito to Cloud Library Cloud Library Management System is an online library system with multiple user groups, including:
Readers. Authors. Librarians. Administrators. Each user group has its own functionalities. Therefore, in addition to managing account information, the system also needs an authentication mechanism to identify the users accessing it.
During the development process, I practiced and tested the following basic functionalities.
Account Registration Users enter the required information on the Cloud Library registration interface.
The application sends a registration request to Amazon Cognito to create an account in the User Pool.
Email Verification After registration, users need to complete the email verification process according to the system configuration.
I tested the verification code input interface and the account verification process before logging in.
Login After the account has been confirmed, users can log in to Cloud Library.
When the login credentials are valid, Amazon Cognito supports authentication and returns the corresponding tokens based on the configured authentication flow.
The application can use the authentication results to identify user sessions and protect functionalities that require users to log in.
Integration with Application Data In Cloud Library, Amazon Cognito handles authentication, while Amazon DynamoDB is used to store business data.
For example, when a user adds a book to their favorites list, the system needs to associate that action with the correct user account.
During testing, I checked the storage of the favorites list and confirmed that the data remained available after logging out and logging back in.
Through this experience, I gained a better understanding of the separate roles of an authentication service and a database within the same application.
4. Distinguishing Between Authentication and Authorization One important distinction I recognized when building a system with multiple account types is the difference between Authentication and Authorization.
Authentication Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity, such as through an email address and password.
Authorization Authorization is the process of determining which actions an authenticated user is permitted to perform within the system.
For example, in Cloud Library:
User Group Functionality Reader View books and save books to the favorites list. Author Submit books for approval. Librarian Perform library management operations. Administrator Perform system administration functions. Amazon Cognito supports authentication and provides identity information.
However, business-level authorization rules still need to be properly enforced by the application and backend, rather than relying solely on hiding or displaying functionalities on the user interface.
This is also an area that I need to continue exploring when the system has multiple user groups with different access permissions.
5. Challenges and Lessons Learned When I first started learning about Amazon Cognito, I needed time to understand the differences between components such as User Pool, App Client, and the various steps in the account verification process.
In addition, connecting the registration and login interfaces to AWS required careful verification of configuration parameters and how the application handled the returned results.
Through practical experience, I identified several important considerations:
Clearly define registration and login methods from the beginning. Thoroughly test the entire process of registration, email verification, login, and logout. Do not store user passwords in business data tables. Distinguish between account authentication and access permission verification. Do not expose sensitive information such as passwords, tokens, or App Client Secrets in publicly accessible source code. When developing functionalities that require users to log in, the backend needs to validate tokens and verify permissions to perform the requested actions. An important lesson for me is that account-related functionalities need to be tested throughout the entire workflow, rather than simply checking whether the login process is successful.
6. Conclusion Through learning about and practicing with Amazon Cognito, I realized that using a managed authentication service helps reduce the amount of work required to build and operate an authentication system independently.
For the Cloud Library Management System project, Amazon Cognito is an important component in the development of user account functionalities.
In addition to learning how to configure User Pool and App Client, I also gained a better understanding of the differences between authentication, authorization, and business data management.
In the future, I would like to further explore token mechanisms, access permission verification, and API protection when integrating Amazon Cognito into real-world applications.
I hope this article provides a useful perspective for those who are new to Amazon Cognito and want to understand how to apply this service to a web application project.

title: Blog 3
content:
Exploring AWS Amplify: My Perspective on Architecture and Practical Considerations 1. What Exactly Is AWS Amplify? Simply put, AWS Amplify is not a separate infrastructure independent of AWS. It is an orchestration layer built on top of familiar core services such as Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Cognito, Amazon DynamoDB, and AWS Lambda.
Instead of manually configuring each service and establishing IAM permissions between services, Amplify combines these processes into a unified platform, allowing frontend and mobile developers to deploy their products more quickly.
Differences Between AWS Amplify Gen 1 and Gen 2 While exploring AWS documentation, I learned that AWS Amplify has two generations: Gen 1 and Gen 2. The main difference lies in their approaches to application development and deployment.
Amplify Gen 1 Primarily uses interactive commands through the Amplify CLI or the Amplify Studio interface. Automatically generates CloudFormation templates behind the scenes to deploy AWS resources. Amplify Gen 2 Adopts a Code-first development approach based on AWS CDK. All backend components, such as Auth, Data, Storage, and Functions, are defined directly using TypeScript. Each team member can use a separate Cloud Sandbox environment for testing without affecting each other’s data. 2. AWS Amplify Architecture and Workflow Looking at the architecture diagram, the operation of AWS Amplify can be divided into two main workflows: the developer’s application deployment workflow and the user’s application access workflow.
Application Deployment Workflow Developers write code in Visual Studio Code and perform a git push to GitHub. GitHub sends a notification (Webhook) to AWS Amplify. AWS Amplify automatically retrieves the latest source code, installs dependencies using npm ci, builds the application using npm run build, and deploys it to the production environment with HTTPS enabled. One feature I find particularly useful is Atomic Deploy. If a new build encounters an error during deployment, the previously deployed version of the website remains operational, helping minimize system interruptions.
User Application Access Workflow When users access the website, the system consists of two main components: Amplify Hosting and Amplify Backend.
Amplify Hosting Amplify Hosting is responsible for deploying and distributing the website’s frontend through a global CDN.
The service supports applications such as:
Single Page Application (SPA): React, Vue. Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Next.js, Nuxt. Amplify Backend Amplify Backend supports four fundamental groups of application functionalities.
Component Functionality AWS Service Authentication Registration, login, authorization, and JWT token issuance. Amazon Cognito Storage Storing images, PDF files, and documents. Amazon S3 Database Storing application data with automatic scalability. Amazon DynamoDB Function Executing server-side logic in response to events. AWS Lambda 3. Common Misconceptions and Practical Considerations While learning about AWS Amplify, I noticed several points that can easily cause confusion for those who are new to this service.
Using Amplify Hosting Does Not Require Amplify Backend Amplify Hosting and Amplify Backend can be used independently.
Developers can use Amplify Hosting exclusively to deploy the application frontend, similar to Vercel or Netlify.
Meanwhile, the backend can connect to existing AWS services such as:
Amazon Cognito. Amazon API Gateway. AWS Lambda. Amazon DynamoDB. Amazon S3. Additionally, the application can also connect to a backend deployed outside AWS.
404 Errors When Refreshing Pages in SPA Applications After deploying an SPA application such as React or Vue, the homepage may work normally.
However, when users access a subpage, such as /books/123, and refresh the page by pressing F5, the system may return a 404 Not Found error.
The reason is that the server cannot find the physical file corresponding to the requested path.
To resolve this issue, the following steps can be performed:
Access the AWS Amplify Console. Select Hosting. Navigate to Rewrites and redirects. Add a 200 (Rewrite) rule to rewrite appropriate SPA paths to /index.html. Be Careful with Frontend Environment Variables The AWS Amplify Console provides an Environment variables section, allowing developers to easily configure information such as API URLs or Amazon Cognito IDs.
However, environment variables beginning with VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ may be bundled into the source code delivered to the user’s browser.
Therefore, sensitive information must never be stored in these variables, such as:
AWS Access Key. AWS Secret Access Key. This is an important security consideration during application development and deployment.
When Should You Avoid Using AWS Amplify? AWS Amplify helps simplify the application deployment process. However, in some cases, manually configuring individual AWS services may provide better control and customization.
Some examples include:
Systems requiring extensive internal network customization with complex VPC architectures. Systems using Microservices architecture on Kubernetes (Amazon EKS). Systems requiring detailed customization of Cache policies on Amazon CloudFront or AWS WAF configurations. In these cases, manually integrating individual AWS services provides developers with greater control over infrastructure design and management.
4. Conclusion AWS Amplify does not replace the need to understand and master core AWS services, but it significantly reduces the time required to transform source code into a fully operational product on the Cloud.
By exploring the workflow from git push to Amplify Hosting and how it connects to the underlying backend components, I gained a better understanding of the application deployment process on AWS.
Understanding the operational architecture of AWS Amplify not only makes application deployment faster but also supports the scaling or separation of infrastructure components as the project grows in the future.

title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Prepare the environment
content:
To prepare for this part of the workshop you will need to:
Deploying a CloudFormation stack Modifying a VPC route table. These components work together to simulate on-premises DNS forwarding and name resolution.
Deploy the CloudFormation stack The CloudFormation template will create additional services to support an on-premises simulation:
One Route 53 Private Hosted Zone that hosts Alias records for the PrivateLink S3 endpoint One Route 53 Inbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC Cloud” to resolve inbound DNS resolution requests to the Private Hosted Zone One Route 53 Outbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC On-prem” to forward DNS requests for S3 to “VPC Cloud” Click the following link to open the AWS CloudFormation console. The required template will be pre-loaded into the menu. Accept all default and click Create stack. It may take a few minutes for stack deployment to complete. You can continue with the next step without waiting for the deployemnt to finish.
Update on-premise private route table This workshop uses a strongSwan VPN running on an EC2 instance to simulate connectivty between an on-premises datacenter and the AWS cloud. Most of the required components are provisioned before your start. To finalize the VPN configuration, you will modify the “VPC On-prem” routing table to direct traffic destined for the cloud to the strongSwan VPN instance.
Open the Amazon EC2 console
Select the instance named infra-vpngw-test. From the Details tab, copy the Instance ID and paste this into your text editor
Navigate to the VPC menu by using the Search box at the top of the browser window.
Click on Route Tables, select the RT Private On-prem route table, select the Routes tab, and click Edit Routes.
Click Add route. Destination: your Cloud VPC cidr range Target: ID of your infra-vpngw-test instance (you saved in your editor at step 1) Click Save changes

title: Proposal
content:
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

title: Test the Gateway Endpoint
content:
Create S3 bucket Navigate to S3 management console In the Bucket console, choose Create bucket In the Create bucket console Name the bucket: choose a name that hasn’t been given to any bucket globally (hint: lab number and your name) Leave other fields as they are (default) Scroll down and choose Create bucket Successfully create S3 bucket. Connect to EC2 with session manager For this workshop, you will use AWS Session Manager to access several EC2 instances. Session Manager is a fully managed AWS Systems Manager capability that allows you to manage your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual machines (VMs) through an interactive one-click browser-based shell. Session Manager provides secure and auditable instance management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
First Cloud AI Journey Lab for indepth understanding of Session manager.
In the AWS Management Console, start typing Systems Manager in the quick search box and press Enter: From the Systems Manager menu, find Node Management in the left menu and click Session Manager: Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is already running in “VPC Cloud” and will be used to test connectivity to Amazon S3 through the Gateway endpoint you just created (s3-gwe).
Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
You have successfully start a session - connect to the EC2 instance in VPC cloud. In the next step, we will create a S3 bucket and a file in it.
Create a file and upload to s3 bucket Change to the ssm-user’s home directory by typing cd ~ in the CLI Create a new file to use for testing with the command fallocate -l 1G testfile.xyz, which will create a file of 1GB size named “testfile.xyz”. Upload file to S3 bucket with command aws s3 cp testfile.xyz s3://your-bucket-name. Replace your-bucket-name with the name of S3 bucket that you created earlier. You have successfully uploaded the file to your S3 bucket. You can now terminate the session.
Check object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console. Click the name of your s3 bucket In the Bucket console, you will see the file you have uploaded to your S3 bucket Section summary Congratulation on completing access to S3 from VPC. In this section, you created a Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to upload an object. The upload worked because the Gateway endpoint allowed communication to S3, without needing an Internet Gateway attached to “VPC Cloud”. This demonstrates the functionality of the Gateway endpoint as a secure path to S3 without traversing the Public Internet.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
